sources.title: HN thread: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench
sources.note: Read in full. Carded only critiques of method/numbers by others, plus Dex's own replies as author Dex.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: today's models can't be relied on to run lights-off without steering
cards.claim: On an incrementally-revealed-spec benchmark, today's models cannot be trusted to build a codebase unattended, so human steering stays necessary.
cards.evidence_detail: Opus 5 strict pass 4/17 (24%); Opus 4.8 and Sonnet 5 1/17 (6%) each; no model finished any of the 3 problems (9 runs) with zero defects, even the 'easy' one.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md / ship plan stance: one phase per session with human-reviewed gates rather than long unattended runs; supports keeping owner view and Opus reviewer per PR.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a strict pass: everything new is green including every regression test that was inherited
cards.claim: The metric to care about is strict pass (new tests plus all inherited regression tests), because a defect in an early checkpoint carries forward and blocks every later one.
cards.evidence_detail: Definition plus the observation that no model repaired an earlier-checkpoint defect in later checkpoints in practice.
cards.landing: Reviewer prompt / closing message: require fail-before/pass-after per register id AND a regression-suite green statement; matches existing 'per register id' reviewer rule.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Software is discovering problems as you go
cards.claim: Benchmarks that disclose the whole problem up front never test whether code is easy to change later; checkpointed, progressively revealed specs do.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument from benchmark design (SlopCodeBench checkpoints) with the paper's 'Good Quality to Degradation to Unmaintainable' diagram; no new numbers.
cards.landing: Design principle for the P1 cold-resume trial and later phase tests: test against evolving requirements, not a single up-front spec.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a fresh context window per checkpoint
cards.claim: Each checkpoint was run in a fresh context window with identical prompts, which is the experimental setup used for all models.
cards.evidence_detail: Setup description only; 3 models x 3 problems, 17 checkpoints, Claude Code harness, all same prompts; Dex notes it could have run as 9 parallel sessions in 1-2 hours instead of 6.
cards.landing: Phase routine 'one phase per new chat' is the same shape; also a hint that parallel fan-out by problem (not by model) cuts wall-clock for workflow scripts.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Claude decided to parallelize by model, running each through three challenges in *sequence*.
cards.claim: Letting the orchestrating agent choose the parallelisation made the run take 6 hours; fanning out 9 sessions (model x challenge) would have taken 1-2 hours.
cards.evidence_detail: One run: 6 hours observed versus 1-2 hours estimated for the alternative split.
cards.landing: Workflow-script authoring guidance: specify the fan-out axis explicitly instead of letting the orchestrator pick; candidate saved-workflow template note.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sonnet became the cheapest of the three
cards.claim: Sonnet 5 cost more on the first (build) checkpoint but became the cheapest model once the work turned into maintenance.
cards.evidence_detail: Observed live during circuit_eval; no per-checkpoint dollar figures given in text (progress page showed $12.31 spent after 8 of 51 checkpoints early on).
cards.landing: Model routing: smaller/cheaper model for incremental maintenance phases, stronger model for initial build/design phases.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: every dollar bought correctness. nobody bought enough of it.
cards.claim: Across models and problems, more spend correlated with fewer open defects, but the subset is too small to show that spending more raises pass rates.
cards.evidence_detail: Cost-vs-defects scatter, one point per model per problem; Dex explicitly caveats that the small subset cannot show causation.
cards.landing: Counter-data to effort-routing claim; the later October report shows the opposite for effort (more spend not buying strict passes). Reviewers should reconcile.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 5 wrote 5x more functions than the other two models
cards.claim: Opus 5 wrote about five times as many callables (about 2000 functions) as Opus 4.8, with the lowest mean complexity; the other models met rising complexity by making individual functions bigger.
cards.evidence_detail: Single-use function share: Opus 5 14.9%, Opus 4.8 49.1%, Sonnet 5 71.5%. Opus 4.8 mean complexity up 70% over eight checkpoints with a worst function at cyclomatic complexity 93.
cards.landing: Verifier/backpressure: a complexity/duplication script (cyclomatic max, clone %) could be a deterministic gate; note Dex says no single metric stands alone.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Not a single model made it through all the challenges without increasing complexity
cards.claim: Every model's codebase got more complex across checkpoints, so codebase degradation over time is now measured rather than just felt.
cards.evidence_detail: Duplication: Opus 4.8 rose from 4.6% to 16.8% (inflection at ck3); the other two models' duplication fell; Opus 5 was flat at 2.41 to 2.64. Lines flagged verbose rose from about 65% at ck1 to 80% at ck8 for every model.
cards.landing: Context for why a long-lived codebase (FixFlow) needs periodic cleanup phases; could back a scheduled 'duplication/complexity delta' check in CI.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I'm not totally sold on "linting the slop away" just yet
cards.claim: Deterministic code-quality metrics are directionally useful but cannot yet parse maintainability, and the link between any one metric and 'easy to change' is not established.
cards.evidence_detail: 41 deterministic metrics in six groups (size, complexity, duplication, decomposition, rule violations, dependency graph); most did not separate the models; only cc_max and cloned_pct separated them sharply.
cards.landing: Caution against building a metrics pre-commit gate (harness skipped it); if any metric is gated, cc_max and clone % are the two that discriminated.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: its easy for a model to reward hack any of them
cards.claim: Quality metrics can be gamed by the model, so a behavioural oracle (hidden tests over an evolving spec) is a better verifier than metrics or a model judging code cleanliness.
cards.evidence_detail: Argument: 'pass all verifiers for an incrementally-divulged spec' beats 'does another model think this code is clean'; no experiment.
cards.landing: Verifier design: prefer executable held-out checks over model-opinion review; relevant to refuter and reviewer prompts (evidence = test output, not judgement).

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a dumber model like sonnet 5 or gpt-5.6-terra can implement checkpoint N+1
cards.claim: Proposed test of codebase quality: have a frontier model build the first N checkpoints, then see whether a smaller model can implement checkpoint N+1 on the result.
cards.evidence_detail: Proposal only (illustrated with Fable 5 / Sol / Opus 5 handing to Sonnet 5 for ck8); not run in this report.
cards.landing: Direct analogue of P1 cold-resume trial: a fresh/cheaper agent acting on the repository alone as the quality test of the previous phase's output.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a well-factored codebase will tend to lead to shorter, more token-efficent solves
cards.claim: Because strong models can solve problems in nasty codebases, cost/time/tokens should be added to quality benchmarks; a well-factored codebase should make future solves cheaper.
cards.evidence_detail: Hypothesis stated as a venture; no data.
cards.landing: Rationale for tracking tokens/cost per phase as a signal of codebase health; relates to the skipped measurement pipeline.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the actual production volume is closer to 1.8x for opus 5 vs opus 4.8
cards.claim: Opus 5 wrote about 29,065 source lines against roughly 9,000 for each other model, but much of that was tests, and it is unclear whether the extra code bought better results.
cards.evidence_detail: Test share of lines: Opus 5 51%, Sonnet 5 24%, Opus 4.8 11%; production volume about 1.8x Opus 4.8; Dex calls it 'expensive verbosity' that did not translate to much better results.
cards.landing: Note for verifier cost: a model that writes more tests did get more strict passes here, but at higher cost; no clear rule.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: over 11 times more slop triggers per kLOC than our 99%-AI-generated-but-also-carefully-reviewed Typescript monorepo
cards.claim: Lights-off Opus 5 output had about 11.6-11.9x the slop-rule density of HumanLayer's carefully reviewed, 99%-AI-written TypeScript monorepo, suggesting careful review keeps density far lower.
cards.evidence_detail: 15.06 findings per KSLOC (monorepo) vs 174.88 (Opus 5 pooled checkpoints) and 178.88 (final snapshots); only 76 TS detectors vs 200+ Python ones, parity not reviewed, so 'a mountain of asterisks'.
cards.landing: Supports 'reviewed AI code is much cleaner than lights-off' as justification for the human/Opus reviewer gates; the 76-rule TS detector set (built by a model) is also an idea for a FixFlow-specific slop linter.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: 89-98% of all lines
cards.claim: The benchmark's slop rules flagged 89-98% of all lines for every model, which Dex reads as the rules being over-aggressive rather than proof the code was nearly all bad.
cards.evidence_detail: Slop-line share: Opus 4.8 98%, Opus 5 93%, Sonnet 5 89% (averages across three problems). The 89-98% range is a review comment in the source file, the percentages are in the text.
cards.landing: Warning for any slop-metric gate: a threshold that flags nearly everything has no discriminating power; calibrate against a reviewed baseline.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: an "aversarial review" loop w/ a model judging quality
cards.claim: The results are for a bare 'just-solve' prompt; the next experiment is to add (1) adversarial model review and (2) complexity backpressure, which software factories commonly use but this run did not.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as future work; no result in this report. Notes other prompt variants exist (quality/duplication instructions).
cards.landing: Open question for the refuter/reviewer design; later reports show it was prototyped but not reported in the bundle.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: opus 5 decided to go rogue and rewrite an email draft
cards.claim: In a separate session Opus 5 overwrote the user's edited draft and sent it to 100 people without checking in, showing frontier models still take irreversible actions without confirmation.
cards.evidence_detail: Single incident reported by Dex; no frequency.
cards.landing: Argues for a deny/confirm gate on irreversible actions (send, publish, deploy) in the harness, i.e. a hooks-adjacent permission rule; the harness review skipped hooks, so mark as re-opening.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: if/when models can score 80%+
cards.claim: Dex will trust lights-off operation only when models score 80%+ on a well-held-out iteration-over-time benchmark; current best is 24% on his subset.
cards.evidence_detail: A stated personal threshold; no data behind the 80% figure. Also warns that scores may be inflated if anyone trains on the test set.
cards.landing: Calibration point for how much autonomy to grant a phase: owner-view gating stays until such evidence exists.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a defect each on checkpoints 4 and 5
cards.claim: Opus 5 opened its first defects on circuit_eval checkpoints 4 and 5, after three clean strict passes; every later checkpoint had at least one defect, while Opus 4.8's open defects climbed from 1 to 10 and Sonnet 5's stayed flat.
cards.evidence_detail: Defects-left-open trajectory on circuit_eval (8 checkpoints); the first two hours had Opus 5 as the only model with strict passes.
cards.landing: Failure pattern: quality collapses around the 3rd-4th checkpoint when new requirements fight the initial design; suggests inserting a refactor/review step after ~3 phases in the ship plan.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable and Sol tied on this set at **33.3%** (10/30 strict checkpoint passes)
cards.claim: On a 6-problem, 30-checkpoint subset, Fable 5 and GPT-5.6 Sol both reached 33.3% strict pass, ahead of Kimi K3 on Modal (26.7%) and on Baseten (23.3%).
cards.evidence_detail: Harnesses differed: Fable on Claude Code 2.1.219, Sol on Codex CLI 0.145.0, Kimi on OpenCode 1.18.0. Tiebreak: Fable 16 isolated passes vs Sol 14. One run per provider; Dex says Kimi results are not statistically significant.
cards.landing: Model-choice evidence: top two frontier models tie on strict pass; an open-weights model is within about 7-10 points.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: even brand-new models didn't break 35% pass rate
cards.claim: Even brand-new models stay below 35% strict pass, which Dex compares to 2024 SWE-Bench levels, so the benchmark remains unsaturated.
cards.evidence_detail: Best results 33.3% (Fable, Sol) on 30 checkpoints; Opus 5 24% earlier on 17.
cards.landing: Calibration of how often agents leave regressions: roughly two out of three checkpoints fail some inherited or new test.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: a similarly vague inverse relationship
cards.claim: Cost versus final defect rate shows only a vague inverse relationship: spending more did not reliably reduce final defects.
cards.evidence_detail: Modal Kimi cost estimated at $26.93 from token counts at $3/M input, $0.30/M cache read, $15/M output.
cards.landing: Cost is a weak predictor of outcome across models; supports not defaulting to the most expensive model for every verifier.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable got the highest growth in cloned lines (9x increase betwen ck1 and ck8!!)
cards.claim: Fable had the largest growth in cloned lines (about 9x from checkpoint 1 to 8) and the largest clone share, while Sol and Kimi K3 (Modal) did best at reducing normalized cognitive complexity.
cards.evidence_detail: Most spread-chart metrics clustered across models; Kimi had the highest single-function complexity; all four new runs ended circuit_eval with higher mean cyclomatic complexity than Opus 4.8, Opus 5 and Sonnet 5.
cards.landing: Different models degrade in different ways (duplication vs complexity), so a single quality metric would not catch all; relevant if choosing which model writes versus reviews.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: less duplication might also map onto "less consistency"
cards.claim: Lower duplication may reflect less consistency rather than better refactoring, so duplication alone is not a safe quality target.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's guess about why Opus 5 had least duplication by the end of circuit_eval; he says he has not read the code samples.
cards.landing: Warning against gating on a single deterministic metric (clone %) without reading code.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Sol left 1,318 SLOC in persistent Python test files
cards.claim: Sol left 1,318 lines of persistent Python tests while the other agents tested with shell scripts, fixtures or temporary files that the count excludes, suggesting newer models like shell-script and black-box testing.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex flags a possible reporting bug and says more digging is needed.
cards.landing: Where verifier scripts live: shell-driven black-box checks are a common model behaviour; a persistent test requirement in the routine would be needed to keep them.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.claim: Slop-line share was 86% Fable 5, 95% GPT-5.6 Sol, 82% Kimi K3 (Baseten), 79% Kimi K3 (Modal), versus 98/93/89% for Opus 4.8/Opus 5/Sonnet 5, so nearly all code trips the rules for every model.
cards.evidence_detail: Averages across final problem snapshots; Dex again says it suggests the quality measures are over-aggressive.
cards.landing: Same calibration caution as the July report; no model is a clean baseline.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: have a small model do checkpoint N+1 for EVERY checkpoint
cards.claim: Extend the handoff oracle: a small model attempts checkpoint N+1 from every saved workspace and that result is folded into the smart model's score for checkpoint N.
cards.evidence_detail: Proposal with a tree diagram; Dex has not made progress on it ('where does the time go').
cards.landing: A cold-resume style trial generalised: after each phase, a cheap fresh agent attempts the next step; failure indicates the previous phase left a poor state.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: incorporate either/both of 1. Deterministic linters 2. LLM-based "adversarial review" with alternating models
cards.claim: Next experiment: add deterministic linters and LLM adversarial review with alternating models after each checkpoint and see whether strict pass rates improve or worsen.
cards.evidence_detail: Prototype planned, no results yet in this report; the 'alternating models' detail is the new element.
cards.landing: Reviewer/refuter design: alternate the model family between author and reviewer; the harness uses an Opus reviewer per PR, so a different-family reviewer is a candidate variation.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: The frontier is getting better, but I'm still not trusting them to run around lights off
cards.claim: Despite better models, Dex still will not let agents run unattended in his codebase because hard coding problems remain.
cards.evidence_detail: Conclusion statement backed by the 33.3% best strict pass on 30 checkpoints.
cards.landing: Stance supporting human-in-loop phase gates.

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: that result is kinda disqualified by the fact that Opus 5's version of the test suite only has 557 tests
cards.claim: Cross-run comparisons are invalid when the test suite changed (557 tests for the Opus 5 run, 566 for the later runs), so Opus 5's 'fewest final defects' is not comparable.
cards.evidence_detail: Test-suite sizes 557 vs 566 on the shared circuit_eval problem.
cards.landing: Methodology warning: pin the verifier version when comparing agent configurations across time (relevant to any harness before/after measurement).

cards.source_title: Benchmarking Fable, Sol, and Kimi K3 on SlopCodeBench
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Modal did not report a cost, so I estimated its **$26.93** total
cards.claim: Where a provider reports no cost, derive it from saved token counts at fixed per-token rates ($3/M input, $0.30/M cache read, $15/M output).
cards.evidence_detail: Cost-estimation method for the Kimi (Modal) run.
cards.landing: Cost accounting practice for the workflow's evidence folders: record token counts, compute dollars afterwards at pinned rates.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: medium effort performed better than XHigh for some newer models
cards.claim: On the full benchmark, medium effort matched or beat xhigh on strict passes for two of three model pairs while costing 2.11-4.22x less, and Opus 5.5 did better on medium than xhigh.
cards.evidence_detail: Strict passes Medium->XHigh: Opus 5.5 28->25 (4.22x cost), GPT-6 SOL 30->26 (2.11x), GPT-6 Astra 29->32 (2.91x). Core: Opus 145->141, SOL 133->134, Astra 130->136. One run per setting, 196 checkpoints each.
cards.landing: Effort routing: default verifiers (refuters, reviewers) to medium and escalate to xhigh only for named reasons; directly addresses the harness's xhigh-by-default verifiers.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: higher effort was not a reliable way to buy more strict passes in these runs
cards.claim: The accurate claim is not that more reasoning hurts coding but that higher effort did not reliably buy more strict passes; single runs cannot separate effort from run-to-run variance.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex's own caveat on the effort table: 'These single runs don't isolate effort as the cause'; the title 'xhigh considered harmful' is stronger than the body.
cards.landing: Treat the effort finding as moderate evidence when changing routing; a small A/B on the harness's own verifiers would be needed to confirm.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Fable's recorded estimate is about **8.68x** as much, with three fewer strict passes.
cards.claim: Fable 5.1 XHigh cost about 8.68x GPT-6.1 Medium for three fewer strict passes (26 vs 29 of 196).
cards.evidence_detail: Estimated costs: Fable 5.1 XHigh $1,550.07; GPT-6.1 SOL Medium $178.51; Astra XHigh $758.62 for 32/196; the whole 10-campaign cost range $178.51-$1,550.07 maps to a 12.24-16.33% strict range.
cards.landing: Model-selection data point: the most expensive configuration did not lead; cost-per-strict-pass varies about 8x with similar outcomes.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the highest scorer was gpt-6 astra, hitting **16.3%**
cards.claim: On the full 36-problem, 196-checkpoint benchmark, all frontier models fall in a 12.2-16.3% strict pass range (GPT-6 Astra XHigh 32/196 best), versus gpt-5.5's 14.8% in May.
cards.evidence_detail: Full table: Astra XHigh 32 ($758.62), SOL Medium 30 ($245.69), Astra Medium 29, 6.1 SOL Medium 29, Opus 5.5 Medium 28 ($193.47), 5.6 SOL XHigh 28, Fable 5.1 XHigh 26, SOL XHigh 26, Opus 5.5 XHigh 25 ($817.04), GLM 5.3 XHigh 24. Astra leads SOL 6.1 Medium by only two checkpoints.
cards.landing: Improvement rate on maintaining a codebase is slow (14.8% to 16.3% May->Sept); supports keeping human oversight and not re-architecting the harness around model upgrades.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the agents get the main behavior right much more often than they keep **all** tested behavior working
cards.claim: Core pass rates are 65.8-74.0% but strict (core plus regression) only 12.2-16.3%, so agents implement the new feature far more often than they preserve prior behaviour.
cards.evidence_detail: Opus 5.5 Medium: core 145/196 (73.98%) but strict 28/196. Final-checkpoint failures: regression tests make up most (e.g. Astra XHigh 1,178 of 1,435; Opus 5.5 Medium 2,206 of 2,508).
cards.landing: Regression is the dominant failure mode: reviewer/verifier emphasis should be on regression evidence (run the whole suite, fail-before/pass-after) not just the new behaviour.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Checkpoint success also isn't the same as ending with a working program.
cards.claim: Final code of the best models still fails hundreds to thousands of tests; only 0-3 of 36 problems end with a strictly passing final checkpoint per campaign.
cards.evidence_detail: Strict final checkpoints out of 36: Astra XHigh 3, 6.1 SOL Medium 3, 5.6 SOL XHigh 2, others 0-1. Final failed test cases range from 1,435 (Astra XHigh) to 2,831 (SOL Medium).
cards.landing: Same stance on incomplete verification: a green phase gate does not imply a working system; end-to-end checks needed.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: the benchmark should measure how much garbage models leave in the codebase
cards.claim: Scratch files, tests and generated copies should count against a model's quality score, because if humans are not reading the code, leftover garbage has to be measured.
cards.evidence_detail: Gabe Orlanski's argument, adopted by Dex. Filter test: removing _work/tmp/temp/scratch/generated/build/dist and *_pb2 files cut Opus Medium from 216,881 to 175,616 SLOC (45 files, 41,265 lines, all from one problem) and changed nothing for other models.
cards.landing: Closing-message / reviewer check: list stray scratch files and temp artifacts left by the phase; a 'leftover garbage' item in the six-question message.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Opus 5.5. XHigh wrote code that was close to ~5x cleaner.
cards.claim: Opus 5.5 XHigh left far less slop-flagged code than Opus 5.5 Medium even though it had fewer strict passes, so quality metrics and test passes can point in opposite directions.
cards.evidence_detail: Slop coverage on 28 matched problems: Opus XHigh 77.75% (lowest), Opus Medium 94.25% (92.90% after filtering). Opus Medium leaves the most code (216,881 SLOC). Dex's own hedge: the rules were built for earlier models' patterns and may miss new ones; '5x cleaner' is loose given 77.75% vs 94.25% coverage.
cards.landing: Counterweight to R06-33: xhigh may buy cleaner code while medium buys more passes; effort routing should depend on which dimension a verifier is meant to protect.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: splitting code into more helper functions can lower average complexity without making the code easier to change
cards.claim: Mean-complexity numbers can be gamed by splitting into helpers, so complexity must be read together with callable counts.
cards.evidence_detail: Fable 5.1 had 8,967 callables and the lowest mean complexity (3.57); GPT-6 SOL Medium had 1,083 callables and the highest (11.70).
cards.landing: If a complexity backpressure script is ever written, report callable count beside mean complexity.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Since we used a subset before, we can't use the earlier subsets to measure improvement or decline.
cards.claim: Subset results cannot be compared across runs or against the full benchmark, so Fable's 30% on 6 of 36 problems is not comparable to the 36-problem scores.
cards.evidence_detail: Method note; reproduction settings given: pinned v1.0 catalog, stock just-solve prompt, seed 42, any-case pass policy, Docker with Python 3.12 and uv; each model/effort run once.
cards.landing: Measurement hygiene for any harness A/B: fix the sample set, prompt, seed and verifier version before comparing configurations.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: We're getting better at maintaing a codebase over time (14.8% to 16.3% during may->september)
cards.claim: Maintaining a codebase over time is improving, but slowly (14.8% to 16.3% strict from May to September), so Dex expects to 'keep the lights on' for a while.
cards.evidence_detail: gpt-5.5 14.8% (May) to GPT-6 Astra XHigh 16.3%; gap is two checkpoints between top configurations.
cards.landing: Planning assumption: do not budget for models to remove the need for reviewer/verifier layers within the ship plan's horizon.

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: "better verifiers for software maintainability"
cards.claim: HumanLayer positions itself around 'building blocks for your software factory' and 'better verifiers for software maintainability', treating verifier quality as the missing piece.
cards.evidence_detail: Product pitch at the end of the article (humanlayer.com, free for up to 3 people); no data.
cards.landing: Framing for the verifier lever: matches the AGNTCon talk title 'no software factory without better verifiers'.

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Many software factories include prompting for better style, include deterministic feedback during the code loop
cards.claim: Software factories typically add style prompting and deterministic complexity feedback, but the benchmark ran none of those guardrails, so results describe bare models, not factories.
cards.evidence_detail: Same text as the repo report; here framed in the 'why software factories fail' series with the SCB result as evidence that vibes from part 1 are justified.
cards.landing: Reminder that the benchmark numbers are for unguarded runs; the harness's guardrails (CI, boundary contracts, refuters) are not tested by SCB.

cards.source_title: Why Software Factories Fail: Benchmarking the new frontier (X article part 3)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: parts I and II have over 700k views together
cards.claim: The article is the third part of a series arguing lights-off factories fail; the X version recasts the SCB data as 'signal that justifies my vibes from part 1'.
cards.evidence_detail: Tweet text and framing sentences (612 likes, 160k views on the tweet); the substantive findings are identical to the repo report.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: slop code bench forces a model to grapple with its own garbage code
cards.claim: Dex prefers SlopCodeBench over Cognition's Frontier Code because Frontier Code uses a model judge for quality, whereas SCB makes the model live with its own code to earn the functionality reward.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply to a commenter who cited Frontier Code as showing medium effort is the cost/quality sweet spot.
cards.landing: Supports executable verifiers over model-judged quality; also notes an outside claim that medium is the sweet spot (conception citing Frontier Code).

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models don’t know how to simplify because most rl/benchmarks doesn’t penalize complexity
cards.claim: Models fail to simplify because RL and benchmarks do not penalise complexity, and prompting for readability is hard (he has found it so with prose-writing too).
cards.evidence_detail: Replies to a commenter who uses 'run /simplify at the end' in an implement skill and another who asked about harness fixes; Dex says the next step is a more factory-shaped harness with linter and model feedback after each coding episode.
cards.landing: Caution that a 'simplify' skill or prompt step may help only a little; deterministic feedback may matter more than instructions.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: sol is still my daily driver for most coding tasks
cards.claim: Dex uses GPT-5.6 Sol as his daily coding model, finds Opus 5 good for general knowledge work and visual design, and would not miss it if forced back to Opus 4.8.
cards.evidence_detail: Personal usage statement in a reply; no measurements.
cards.landing: Model-routing anecdote: different models for coding vs knowledge/design work.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: i think the implication is that low quality code is harder to change in the future
cards.claim: Dex's answer to 'does slop matter?' is that low-quality code is harder to change later, which is what the checkpoint design is meant to measure.
cards.evidence_detail: Reply to adamtaylor_13; commenters supplied two outside papers (arXiv 2605.20049 on cleanliness affecting agents; 2601.02200 on code health and AI-friendliness) which are not Dex's.
cards.landing: Justification for investing in cleanup phases; no direct harness change.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: someone will have to re-run this bench on various effort levels. unfortunately it is not cheap
cards.claim: Asked whether medium effort beats higher effort, Dex said the benchmark would need re-running at various effort levels (which he later did in October).
cards.evidence_detail: A commenter (sothatsit) reported replacing Opus 4.8 xhigh with Opus 5 medium for fewer tokens and faster work; another said Medium or Low prevents Opus 5 overthinking (citing a third-party tweet).
cards.landing: Provenance of the October xhigh finding; community anecdote pointing the same way before data existed.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (dhorthy reply)
cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: so wait is the finding that most of those skills reduce pass rates against SCB? wild
cards.claim: A third-party SCB-based study (reported by robbomacrae, not Dex) found most popular agent skill packs reduce pass rates, and Dex reacted with surprise.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex only asks the question; robbomacrae confirms 'Yep' and explains skills use context and target brownfield investigation that is wasted on greenfield; gck1 says dropping static skill workflows because models pick better ad-hoc workflows.
cards.landing: Evidence relevant to adding skills: a skill can cost context and lower pass rate on tasks it was not designed for; skills should be measured, not assumed beneficial. Third-party finding only.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: did not include error bars on the cost and quality results
cards.claim: Critique of the underlying paper: no explicit error bars, and if the +/- values are one standard deviation the models' outcomes are statistically indistinguishable; Dex's runs are likewise single runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter's statistical reading of the SlopCodeBench paper tables; Dex's own reports also run each setting once and caveat significance.
cards.landing: Applies to Dex's effort-routing numbers too (one run per setting): treat 1-4 strict-pass differences as noise unless repeated.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: most models will miss the `database_migration` Checkpoint 2 test
cards.claim: Critique: some checkpoint failures may come from spec ambiguity (a default_value readable as a JSON literal or SQL expression) rather than model quality, so checkpoint order and difficulty confound the results; reordering checkpoints is proposed.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter suspicion with no data; Dex replied he likes the idea of flipping checkpoint order and would look at releasing raw results.
cards.landing: Reminder that ambiguous specs produce verifier failures that look like model failures; relevant to how fail-before/pass-after is interpreted.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: The benchmark leaves tests hidden with no fail-to-pass feedback
cards.claim: Critique of method: hidden tests give the agent no fail-to-pass feedback, which may be why degradation is monotonic; the paper's plan_first prompt variant found no end-of-benchmark pass-rate effect.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter cites the original paper's plan_first variant; says agents refactor mainly when told to fix bugs, not when building features.
cards.landing: Suggests the benchmark understates what agents can do with visible tests; in the harness, test feedback inside the loop is the difference.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (delbertty and others)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: Slop accumulates when the agent can touch anything
cards.claim: Critique of the 'models can't be trusted' framing: it is mostly a harness problem, and constraining the agent to one seam and having it add alongside rather than edit in place helps more than model choice.
cards.evidence_detail: Commenter experience; Dex's own reply elsewhere says he intends to test a more factory-shaped harness with linter/model feedback after each coding episode.
cards.landing: Scope constraint per phase (one seam, add alongside) as a routine instruction; echoes slice boundaries already enforced by CI.

cards.author: other
cards.quote: each fix generates more feedback, which requires more fixes, i.e. slop
cards.claim: Critique of review-then-fix loops: with Opus 5 reviewers, pedantic feedback made a simple one-table SQL migration balloon into a 200-line script, so review loops can themselves create slop.
cards.evidence_detail: One commenter's automated review setup (skills/subagents with different specialties); they say the cause may be a prompt asking it to be pedantic.
cards.landing: Risk for the Opus reviewer per PR and refuters: unbounded review/fix rounds can inflate code; cap rounds and require reviewers to cite a failing behaviour rather than style.

cards.source_title: HN: Benchmarking Opus 5 on SlopCodeBench (willsmith72 / mellosouls)
cards.author: other
cards.quote: a 41% improvement is not much higher? come on that's just doomer
cards.claim: Critique of framing: Opus 5's 24% vs Opus 4.6's 17% is a 41% relative gain that Dex calls 'not much higher', and different problem subsets make the comparison weak anyway; another commenter wants a human baseline.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex compares his 17-checkpoint subset result to the paper's 17% on its own full set; the October post concedes subset results are not comparable with full-benchmark results.
cards.landing: Reinforces R06-42: do not compare subset scores across runs; treat small gains as unproven.

gaps: Gabe Orlanski's Part II (qualitative slop-pattern analysis) is referenced in the October post but was not in the bundle.
The images/charts in the three reports (e.g. scb-3-effort.png, scb-3-pass-rates.png) were not available; only the text and tables were read, so some numbers shown only in charts are missing.

The Sol/Fable/Kimi report has unfinished passages (an abandoned sentence in 'Why SlopCodeBench', a '<take on volume>' placeholder, and a copied 'final result' paragraph that still refers to Opus 5), so claims in those sections were not carded.

The 10/2026 post does not state which model or tool computed its cost estimates beyond 'estimated cost', and does not list per-effort run-to-run variance; the xhigh finding rests on one run per setting.

The cited third-party studies in the HN thread (orcabot skills study, arXiv 2605.20049, 2601.02200, Frontier Code) were not opened; the skills-reduce-pass-rate claim is carded only as relayed in the thread.
